title: Prayer Robotics Kits
subject: Constitutional Law
stem:
BARMATRIX Q#: 20714_prayer_robotics_kits

After reports that teenagers at weekend robotics competitions are injuring themselves while soldering circuit boards, Congress enacts a provision distributing free soldering-safety kits to participants in public programs and private youth academies. The kits contain goggles, burn pads, and safety cards; they contain no prayer, worship material, or religious instruction. In many states, most private youth academies are church-affiliated. Lydia, a federal taxpayer, challenges the provision, arguing that it unconstitutionally supports religious entities.

Does Lydia have standing to make the challenge?

Source row reviewed: BARMATRIX Q# 20714, Constitutional Law, official key B.

---
call: Does Lydia have standing to make the challenge?

choices.A: No, because Lydia has not shown the required nexus between her taxpayer status and the safety-kit expenditures.
choices.B: Yes, because any federal taxpayer may challenge a congressional spending authorization.
choices.C: No, because there is no proof that any money freed up by the free kits will be used for religious purposes.
choices.D: Yes, because the challenge alleges a possible violation of a specific constitutional limit on Congress’s spending power.

rightExplanation:
D is correct. Lydia is not relying on a general taxpayer grievance. She is challenging a congressional spending provision and claiming that the spending violates a specific constitutional limit on that spending power.

Gold Key: Federal taxpayers generally cannot sue just because tax money is being spent, but the Flast exception allows standing for a challenge to congressional taxing-and-spending action when the claim invokes a specific constitutional limit on that spending power. The Establishment Clause is the classic trigger.

Silver Key: Lock the call as standing, not merits. Do not ask whether the robotics kits are actually unconstitutional; ask whether this taxpayer is allowed into court to make that claim.

---

c3.label: B — CUT
c3.text: “Any federal taxpayer” is an overclaim. The word any is the visible breaker.

c3.label: C — CUT
c3.text: The choice answers a merits/funding-use question. The call asks standing.

c3.label: A vs D — CALL with Gold Key
c3.text:
Both speak the language of taxpayer standing. The axis is whether the spending-limit nexus is missing or supplied. The Gold Key resolves it: congressional spending + Establishment Clause claim supplies the exception. D survives.

---

studentScript: This is a standing call. Cut 'any taxpayer' as too broad. Cut saved-money proof as merits, not standing. Use the Gold Key: congressional spending plus Establishment Clause is the taxpayer-standing exception. Pick D.

A.signal: After the Gold Key, the required connection is supplied rather than missing.
A.lawyer: Flast uses a nexus/logical-link structure for congressional spending claims under the Establishment Clause; this fact pattern satisfies that exception.

B.signal: The word 'any' makes the taxpayer-standing rule too broad.
B.lawyer: Federal taxpayer standing is generally barred; Flast is a narrow exception.

C.signal: The choice asks how recipients will use saved money; the call asks whether Lydia may sue.
C.lawyer: The Flast standing inquiry does not require proof that freed private funds will be spent for religious purposes.

D.signal: Congressional spending plus a specific Establishment Clause limit is the narrow taxpayer-standing exception.

goldKeys.statement: Federal taxpayers generally lack standing, but they may challenge a congressional taxing-and-spending enactment when the claim alleges violation of a specific constitutional limit on that spending power; the Establishment Clause is the classic trigger.
goldKeys.trigger: Federal taxpayer + congressional spending + Establishment Clause claim.

silverKeys.statement: On a taxpayer-standing call, separate entry-to-court from whether the aid is unconstitutional.
silverKeys.trigger: The call asks whether the taxpayer has standing.

remediation.title: Taxpayer Standing: Narrow Door, Not Open Gate
remediation.studentMove: Cut 'any taxpayer' overclaims, then check the narrow spending-power/Establishment trigger.
remediation.tinyRule: General no standing; Flast exception for congressional spending plus Establishment Clause.
remediation.trap: Treating all taxpayer challenges as allowed, or treating merits proof as standing proof.
